must.text: Confirms pause is not set by describing the Kafka resource and looking for status condition type ReconciliationPaused, which is how a paused custom resource is reported.
set_evidence: The `type` condition changes to `ReconciliationPaused` at the `lastTransitionTime`.

must.text: Checks the maintenance window against the Cluster Operator reconciliation interval: the window must be at least as long as that interval, and the interval defaults to 120000 ms (STRIMZI_FULL_RECONCILIATION_INTERVAL_MS).
set_evidence: maintenance time windows must be at least as long as the interval between reconciliations.
`STRIMZI_FULL_RECONCILIATION_INTERVAL_MS`:: Optional, default is 120000 ms.

must_not.text: States that maintenanceTimeWindows hold every broker roll, including a spec.kafka.config edit, until the window opens.
must_not.condition: Counts when the window is described as gating this config roll. Saying the window still gates automatic certificate renewals does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Automatic certificate-renewal rolls are restricted by the window; this num.network.threads edit is not.

must_not.text: Explains this Thursday config roll by the maintenance window being shorter than the reconciliation interval.
must_not.condition: Counts only if that length rule is given as the cause of this config restart. Mentioning the rule as a separate check for certificate renewals does not count.
must_not.near_miss: A window shorter than the reconciliation interval can let a renewal reconciliation fall outside the window; it does not release a user config edit early.

reference: The Sunday window never applied to this edit. maintenanceTimeWindows cover automatic certificate renewals and the rolls those renewals cause. A user-driven change to the Kafka resource, including spec.kafka.config, restarts brokers immediately; user-driven restarts are not restricted by the window. The cron is UTC, and Thursday 15:00 UTC is outside "* * 0-5 ? * SUN *", so the window was closed. Pause is not the cause: annotations are empty, and a paused resource would ignore the edit and show condition ReconciliationPaused rather than roll. Read kubectl get kafka payments -n pay -o yaml and kubectl get pods -n pay. A window shorter than the reconciliation interval (STRIMZI_FULL_RECONCILIATION_INTERVAL_MS, default 120000 ms) can let a renewal miss the window; this window is six hours and this was not a renewal. Leave the window for certificate renewals. The next config edit will also roll as soon as it is saved.
correct_alternative: Same cause: num.network.threads is a user-driven Kafka resource change, and those restarts ignore maintenanceTimeWindows. The cron is interpreted in UTC, and Thursday is outside the Sunday window. kubectl describe kafka payments -n pay shows no ReconciliationPaused condition, so strimzi.io/pause-reconciliation is not hiding anything; a true pause would ignore the spec instead of restarting pods. Manual Cluster CA or Clients CA updates, and CN or SAN changes, are also user-initiated and roll immediately. Keep the Sunday window for automatic renewals, and make sure it stays longer than the 120000 ms reconciliation interval. Accept this roll.
generic: Daytime broker restarts usually mean a certificate expired or a probe failed. Widen the cron so it covers Thursday, cordon the nodes, and raise terminationGracePeriodSeconds. Restart the Cluster Operator and check etcd latency before editing broker config again.

Pause is a discriminator, not the cause.

After size went from 1000Gi to 2000Gi, Kubernetes grew the persistent volumes; kubectl get pv already shows 2000Gi. When that resize completes, the operator restarts every pod that uses the resized volume, and the restart is automatic. generic: The log.retention.hours change forced the rolling restart, and shorter retention is making the log cleaner hot. Check broker logs, raise memory, and increase num.io.threads. If a pod is slow to come back, delete it so the StatefulSet recreates the disk.

reference: CpuCapacityGoal failed the proposal: utilization 615.21 is above allowed capacity 420.00 at threshold 0.70, so payments-rebalance is NotReady with OptimizationFailureException. Those figures are percentages of one virtual CPU per broker, not core counts, and they do not map onto the number 4. That virtual CPU has the cycles of KafkaNodePool.spec.resources.limits.cpu, and the percentage display does not change the utilization-to-capacity ratio. excludedTopics payments-audit does not drop this load: excluded topics are not moved, but their CPU still counts. The exception's remedy is to add at least 3 brokers with the same CPU capacity as broker-0, not 3 brokers of 100 cores. Requests are 500m and limits are 4, so also set requests equal to limits, or set spec.cruiseControl.brokerCapacity.cpu to the real capacity, or CPU goals are not guaranteed accurate. Then annotate strimzi.io/rebalance=refresh and wait for PendingProposal or ProposalReady. Rollback: if a rebalance is already Rebalancing, annotate strimzi.io/rebalance=stop and wait for Stopped; finished moves stay. Revert a requests edit on the node pool. Remove any added brokers only with remove-brokers, after partitions are off them. Do not set skipHardGoalCheck or drop CpuCapacityGoal to force the proposal.
correct_alternative: Set the node pool CPU requests equal to the limit of 4 and add at least 3 brokers with the same CPU capacity as broker-0. The exception's 100.00 is one virtual CPU (the cycles of the node pool limit), not 100 cores, and the ratio is unchanged by that display. payments-audit stays in the CpuCapacityGoal math, so the regex does not clear the error. If quota blocks raising requests, set spec.cruiseControl.brokerCapacity.cpu to "4" instead, and still add those three brokers. Annotate payments-rebalance with strimzi.io/rebalance=refresh and wait for PendingProposal or ProposalReady. Roll back a running rebalance with strimzi.io/rebalance=stop until Stopped, and remove extra brokers only after remove-brokers shows they have no partitions.
generic: Cruise Control is failing because the brokers are out of CPU. Raise the node pool limit from 4 to 100 cores to match the 100.00 in the error, and exclude payments-audit so its CPU is ignored. Restart Cruise Control and approve the rebalance. If it still fails, turn off hard goals and run a full rebalance overnight.

reference: Annotate before each scale. Scale-up takes the lowest available id in strimzi.io/next-node-ids, so set that annotation to [20] (no free id under 20; id 0 is free) and then kubectl scale kafkanodepool brokers --replicas=5. Scale-down removes the highest id in strimzi.io/remove-node-ids. A single id is how you remove one specific node, so set [4]. A range that also contains 7 removes 7. Auto-rebalance is off, so before the replica drop apply a KafkaRebalance labeled strimzi.io/cluster: orders with mode remove-brokers and brokers: [4]. Only after that reassignment finishes and node 4 has no live partitions, kubectl scale kafkanodepool brokers --replicas=4. If the annotation is missing, misformatted, the scale-up range is exhausted, or the scale-down range matches no in-use node, the operator uses the default: the lowest free id in the cluster on the way up, and the highest id in the pool on the way down. Ids 20 and 4 are inside 0-999, so no max-id setting is required.
correct_alternative: Put the ranges on the KafkaNodePool as metadata.annotations instead of kubectl annotate: strimzi.io/next-node-ids: "[20,21]" (the lowest available id is still 20) and strimzi.io/remove-node-ids: "[4]". Scale replicas from 4 to 5 only after next-node-ids is stored. For the removal, apply a KafkaRebalance with mode remove-brokers, brokers: [4], and label strimzi.io/cluster: orders. Wait until node 4 has no live partitions, then scale replicas from 5 to 4. Do not put 5, 6, or 7 in the remove range. A missing or misformatted range falls back to the lowest free id on scale-up and the highest id in the pool on scale-down.
generic: Increase spec.replicas from 4 to 5 and later decrease it to 4. Kafka assigns the next broker ids itself, so the new pod is the next ordinal and the scale-down drops the oldest pod. kubectl delete pod orders-brokers-4 before the scale so that node is the one that goes. No extra annotation is required.
note: Pod names follow the cluster-pool-node id pattern in the scale-up procedure. Node ids 4, 5, 6, 7 and the target id 20 are invented; id 0 being free is part of the premise so a range such as [0-20] would not select 20. m1 accepts any next-node-ids range whose lowest available id is 20, including [20,21]. m2 requires a single-id remove range because the highest id in a wider in-use range would be removed. The ID procedure's prose says reserved.broker-max.id, while the example YAML in the same page says reserved.broker.max.id, and the Kafka 4.3 docs list reserved.broker.max.id as removed for KRaft. This scenario stays inside 0-999 and does not ask for that property. No any_of group.

Prefer raising pool brokers spec.replicas from 6 to 12: that is a scaling event, and add-brokers auto-rebalance redistributes partitions with no hand-written KafkaRebalance. The other design is a new broker-only pool plus a KafkaRebalance mode add-brokers listing the new ids, because creating a pool does not trigger auto-rebalance. 480 partitions at replication factor 3 is 1440 replicas: about 240 per broker now, about 120 per broker on 12 brokers (tolerance 100-140). Do not scale the controller pool; controller scaling is not supported. Still missing: bytes used on each broker disk, and CPU or network headroom. Twice the brokers does not help if the disks are already full.

Creating the pool is not an auto-rebalance scaling event, even though add-brokers is configured; the KafkaRebalance is what moves the replicas. The other valid path is spec.replicas 6 to 12 on pool brokers, which does trigger auto-rebalance. 1440 replicas in total, about 120 per broker after the doubling (tolerance 100-140). Leave the 3 controllers alone. Ask for current disk bytes per broker and CPU headroom before freezing the count.
generic: Add virtual machines until the cluster looks comfortable and raise the replication factor if you need more safety. Spread leaders with rack awareness and give the JVM about half the node memory.

reference: Uncompressed logical data is 80 MiB/s for 48 hours: 13500 GiB. At replication factor 3 that is 40500 GiB across the cluster (tolerance 38000-43000), or about 5060 GiB on each of 8 brokers (tolerance 4700-5400), before headroom. audit is replication factor 1, so the brokers cannot use ephemeral storage. Use one persistent-claim per broker of that size plus headroom. JBOD volumes that sum to the same size are the other valid layout, and the one Strimzi recommends when a broker has several disks. Do not plan to lower the size later; decreasing a persistent volume is not supported. Grow by increasing size. Controllers get a single metadata volume; more controller disks do not enlarge the metadata log. Still missing: compression ratio, and the free-space percent to hold back.
correct_alternative: Same byte total, about 40500 GiB uncompressed and replicated, about 5060 GiB per broker before headroom (tolerances 38000-43000 GiB and 4700-5400 GiB). Put that on JBOD persistent volumes per broker instead of one claim. Still not ephemeral, because audit is replication factor 1. Later growth is a larger size, or a new JBOD volume after the metadata volume is pinned. Do not decrease size. Removing a JBOD disk is allowed only after its partitions are moved. Controllers stay on one metadata volume. Ask for the compression ratio and the free-space target before ordering disks.
generic: Use the platform default storage class and add brokers if the disks fill up. A few days of retention is enough for most clusters. Watch disk usage in Prometheus and expand the cluster when alerts fire.

The reference picks the single claim; the alternative picks JBOD. m1 and m2 are arithmetic and missing inputs, not passages. 80 MiB/s times 48 times 3600 is 13824000 MiB, which is 13500 GiB, times 3 is 40500 GiB, divided by 8 is 5062.5 GiB. audit's few KiB/s are ignored in the total on purpose. must.text: Main diagnosis: the HTTP consumer is created on one pay-bridge pod, and later requests for that consumer are landing on other pods, where the consumer state is absent, so the request fails. Produce succeeding does not contradict this.
set_evidence: If a request is routed to a different instance, the consumer state is not available and the request fails.

must.text: Ranks session affinity, or another routing strategy that keeps every request for one consumer on the pod that created it, as the fix. Adding replicas without that pinning does not fix consume.
set_evidence: your networking layer must support session affinity or another routing strategy that ensures requests for the same consumer are consistently routed to the correct instance.

must.text: Treats produce as a negative check: producer requests are stateless, so any bridge pod can serve them, and a healthy produce path does not show that consumer routing is fine.
set_evidence: Producer requests are stateless. Any instance can handle a produce request.

must.text: Separates a pod restart from this outage: if a bridge pod restarts, only the consumers created on that pod are lost and clients must recreate them. Pods have not restarted, and the failure follows creates while all endpoints stay ready, so this is not the restart case.
set_evidence: the consumers created on that instance are lost. This behavior is equivalent to a Kafka client process stopping. Client applications must recreate the consumers and resume processing.

must.text: Names the read-only checks that confirm the winning hypothesis: spec.replicas is 3, pay-bridge-ext has sessionAffinity None (no sticky rule on the load balancer), and the endpoints object lists all three pods.
must.source: read-only checks from the question; sessionAffinity is a Kubernetes Service field, not stated in the bridge pages
must.not_indexed_note: The bridge pages require session affinity or equivalent pinning but do not name the Service sessionAffinity field or the kubectl checks.

must_not.text: States that produce requests also have to stick to one bridge pod, so the working produce path means routing is fine.
must_not.condition: Counts when stated as a fact about this bridge. Saying that a restart drops consumers on that pod does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Producer requests are stateless and any bridge instance can handle them; only consumer requests have to stay on one pod.

must_not.text: Recommends raising spec.consumer.timeoutSeconds above 60 as the fix for these sub-second consumer-not-found errors.
must_not.condition: Counts only if raising the timeout is the recommended fix or part of it. Mentioning timeoutSeconds as a setting that was already checked does not count.
must_not.near_miss: timeoutSeconds is already 60 and the failures return in well under a second, which is a routing miss, not a long poll.

reference: The consumer is created on one of the three bridge pods. Every later request for that consumer has to hit that same pod; if it does not, the consumer state is not there and the call fails. pay-bridge-ext is a LoadBalancer with sessionAffinity None, so consume requests are spread and about two thirds miss. Produce keeps working because those requests are stateless and any pod can take them. A bridge restart would also drop consumers, but only the ones that lived on the restarted pod, and nothing has restarted. Confirm replicas is 3, sessionAffinity is None, and all three endpoints are ready. Fix by pinning each consumer to one pod (Service session affinity, or another strategy that routes on the consumer). Do not raise timeoutSeconds and do not add replicas without pinning. After a future pod restart, clients must recreate the consumers that were on that pod.
correct_alternative: Same cause: the consumer object lives on one HTTP Bridge instance, and a request that lands elsewhere fails because that state is not on the other pod. Instead of Service sessionAffinity, put a gateway in front of pay-bridge-ext that always routes one consumer id to the same pod. Leave produce on a plain load balancer; any instance can produce. Keep timeoutSeconds at 60. Clients still have to recreate a consumer if its pod restarts.
generic: Intermittent 404s usually mean the bridge is overloaded or the consumer timed out. Raise consumer.timeoutSeconds, add replicas, and check that the LoadBalancer has all endpoints. Kafka rebalance delays can also surface as missing consumers.
note: any_of: none. The 404 line and the 30ms timing are invented; the Service and endpoint listing follow ordinary kubectl output, not a Strimzi sample. m5 is the read-only check and is not in the bridge pages. m2 lists two documented pinning styles as separate covering sets, not alternatives the judge must pick between. Closest open family is arch-strimzi-external-access-gateway, which is about Kafka listener exposure, not HTTP Bridge consumer affinity.

must.text: Main diagnosis: changing validityDays does not renew the cluster CA now. The new 730-day value is applied only the next time the certificate is renewed, so the unchanged notAfter is expected.
set_evidence: Changing the `validityDays` does not trigger immediate certificate renewal. The updated value is applied the next time the certificate is renewed, either automatically or through manual renewal.

must.text: Explains that renewalDays is how many days before expiry the renewal window opens, and that changing it triggers renewal only when the certificate falls inside that window. With 45 days left and renewalDays 10, pay-kafka is outside the window, so cutting renewalDays from 30 to 10 delays renewal rather than starting it.
set_evidence: Changes to `renewalDays` may trigger renewal earlier if the new value places the certificate within the renewal window.
Cluster and clients CA certificates generated by the Cluster Operator auto-renew at the start of their respective certificate renewal periods.

must.text: Renews now by annotating secret pay-kafka-cluster-ca-cert with strimzi.io/force-renew=true. A renewed certificate keeps the same private key, so this is not a key replacement.
set_evidence: you can use the `strimzi.io/force-renew` annotation to manually renew one or both of these certificates before the certificate renewal period starts.

must.text: After the new certificate exists, points external clients at the new cluster CA certificate and rechecks notBefore and notAfter with openssl x509 -noout -dates on pay-kafka-cluster-ca-cert.
set_evidence: Update client configurations to trust the new cluster CA certificate.

must_not.text: Recommends strimzi.io/force-replace on secret pay-kafka-cluster-ca (the private key) in order to apply validityDays 730.
must_not.condition: Counts when force-replace of the cluster CA key is the recommended way to renew or to apply the new validity. Naming force-replace as the separate key-replacement procedure does not count.
must_not.near_miss: force-renew on pay-kafka-cluster-ca-cert renews the certificate and keeps the same private key; force-replace on pay-kafka-cluster-ca generates a new key.

must_not.text: States that lowering renewalDays makes the Cluster Operator renew the CA sooner.
must_not.condition: Counts when a smaller renewalDays is described as an earlier renewal for this certificate. Saying that a larger renewalDays can pull a certificate into the window does not count.
must_not.near_miss: renewalDays is the number of days before expiry when renewal starts; raising it can trigger renewal earlier if the certificate enters that window.

reference: validityDays is not a renew button. The CA certificate stays the one that expires on 10 Jan 2027 until the next renewal, and only then does 730 days apply. renewalDays is the window before that expiry, not a renewal interval. The certificate is 45 days from expiry and the window is now 10 days, so it is outside the window; dropping renewalDays from 30 to 10 moved the start later, which is why nothing rolled. To renew today without changing the key, annotate secret pay-kafka-cluster-ca-cert with strimzi.io/force-renew=true. The new certificate uses the same private key. Put that new CA certificate into external client truststores and confirm notBefore and notAfter with openssl x509 -noout -dates on the secret. Do not force-replace pay-kafka-cluster-ca.
correct_alternative: If 10 January is soon enough, do not annotate anything. Leave renewalDays at 10 and validityDays at 730. Automatic renewal starts when the certificate enters that 10-day window, still on the same private key, and 730 days is applied then. Clients still have to trust the new CA certificate once it is issued. Check the dates with the same openssl command so you can see that notAfter has not moved yet.
generic: The CA did not roll because the Cluster Operator is stuck or the cert-manager issuer is missing. Delete the cluster CA secret so it is recreated, restart the operator, and set renewalDays lower so it renews more often. Roll the brokers manually.
note: openssl notBefore and notAfter follow the dates the renew procedure says the command prints; the calendar values are invented so that 45 days remain. No maintenance window is set, on purpose: the manual-renew procedure says a force-renew waits for a maintenance window, while the maintenance-window page says manual CA updates are not held for the window. This scenario does not depend on either claim. m2's 45-versus-10 comparison is the renewal-window rule applied to the question.

Set spec.kafka.authorization.type to simple. That denies every client that has no ACL, and the other services have no KafkaUser yet, so do not flip the switch alone. In that same Kafka change, list superUsers for the principals that must keep working (they bypass ACL checks). Apply the KafkaUsers before or with that change; they stay NotReady until simple authorization exists and then become Ready. Confirm with kubectl get kafkausers -o wide that READY is True. generic: NotReady means the User Operator has not reconciled yet. Delete and recreate the KafkaUser, check the Entity Operator pod, and restart it. ACL names are case sensitive, so change Read to read. Authorization can be enabled later once traffic is quiet.

set_evidence: The lock is released automatically once its duration elapses, making the record available to another delivery attempt.

must_not.text: Deletes invoice-dispatch to clear the stuck locks.

must_not.near_miss: kafka-share-groups.sh --describe is the read-only check, and only a share group with no active members can be deleted.

must_not.near_miss: The lock duration only bounds how long one delivery attempt holds the record; the cap on how many records may be acquired at once is the separate limit.

reference: The group is not caught up. describe shows LAG still in the tens of thousands, and START-OFFSET is only the earliest in-flight offset. Each invoices partition may have only group.share.partition.max.record.locks records acquired at once (200 here). A locked record is unavailable to the other share consumers. When the cap is hit, fetches return no further records until some locks are released or time out. Twenty-four workers that ack only after a 2 second call can hold that many. Several consumers on one partition is normal for a share group; --members showing that does not explain the empty fetches. Lock expiry is a different fault: the default lock is 30 seconds (share.record.lock.duration.ms) and on expiry the record is delivered again. A 2 second call does not hit that. Confirm with kafka-share-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka-1:9092 --describe --group invoice-dispatch and --state. Do not delete the group. Unblock by raising the cap or acknowledging sooner. Lengthening the lock keeps the cap full longer.

Leave group.share.partition.max.record.locks at 200 and make the workers acknowledge or release as soon as the HTTP call is queued, instead of holding the acquisition lock for the whole 2 seconds. Fetches yield records again once the acquired count drops. Still confirm LAG with kafka-share-groups.sh --describe --group invoice-dispatch, and do not treat the shared partition assignment as a bug. Do not raise the lock duration and do not delete the group.
generic: Empty polls usually mean the consumers are caught up or the group is rebalancing. Restart the 24 workers, increase max.poll.records, and add partitions so each consumer gets its own. Check broker disk and under-replicated partitions.

must.text: Main cause: AbortableException requires aborting the transaction and resetting the consumer position, and the catch block only aborts.

must.text: Discards and recreates the producer and the consumer so the group rebalances, fetches the last committed offset, and rewinds to the state before the aborted transaction.
set_evidence: As part of recreating the consumer, the consumer group will rebalance and fetch the last committed offset, which has the effect of rewinding back to the state before the transaction aborted.

must.text: Or refetches the committed offset, since the consumer does not rewind on its own, and seeks the consumer back to it.
set_evidence: the consumer has to refetch the committed offset because it does not automatically rewind
`KafkaConsumer.seek` to rewind the current position

must.text: Sets enable.auto.commit=false on the consumer.
set_evidence: The consumer configuration must include `isolation.level=read_committed` and `enable.auto.commit=false`.

must.text: Moves transactional.id onto the producer and removes it from the consumer, because only the producer has that configuration.
set_evidence: Only the producer has the `transactional.id` configuration.

must_not.text: Calls commitTransaction again after AbortableException, or keeps polling without resetting the position.
must_not.condition: Counts when commit is retried or the consumer is left at its current position. abortTransaction followed by a rewind to the committed offset does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Abort the transaction and reset the consumer position so the aborted batch is reprocessed.

must_not.text: Says putting transactional.id on the consumer is what rewinds the position after an abort.
must_not.condition: Counts when the consumer-side transactional.id is treated as the rewind. Setting it on the producer, including so a restart aborts the previous instance's transaction, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Only the producer has transactional.id, and the consumer position still has to be reset explicitly after an abort.

reference: AbortableException means abort the transaction and reset the consumer position. abortTransaction() does not rewind the consumer, so the following polls skip the batch and a read_committed reader of orders-out never sees it. The last committed offset is still the one from the previous successful transaction. enable.auto.commit must be false; it is true here, so offsets can move outside the transaction. transactional.id on the consumer does nothing. Put transactional.id=order-copier-0 on the producer only; a restart with that id aborts the previous instance's open transaction. Fix: abort, then either recreate the producer and the consumer (the rebalance fetches the committed offset and rewinds) or refetch that offset and seek back, then reprocess. Keep the same transactional.id. Verify that position() matches the committed offset from before the failure and that each missing order id shows up once on orders-out. If a seek landed in the wrong place, seek again to the offset saved from position() beforehand. Do not redeploy the old catch block.
correct_alternative: Keep the same producer object. On AbortableException call abortTransaction, then KafkaConsumer.committed for the assigned orders partitions and seek to those offsets, and reprocess. Also set enable.auto.commit=false and move transactional.id=order-copier-0 to the producer; the consumer setting does nothing. Check position() against the committed offset before the next commit, and seek back to a saved offset if the first seek was wrong.
generic: AbortableException means the broker rejected the batch. Retry commitTransaction, raise transaction.timeout.ms, and restart the pod. The consumer will continue from its latest offset on its own. Auto commit should stay on so progress is not lost.
note: any_of m2a/m2b: recreate both clients, or refetch the committed offset and seek. The log line's message text is invented; the exception class is the documented AbortableException. enable.auto.commit=true and transactional.id on the consumer are invented misconfiguration. design.md also says a sophisticated copier can 'choose not to use KafkaConsumer.committed' and then seek, which contradicts the earlier sentence that the consumer must refetch the committed offset. The rubric follows the refetch sentence and the recreate policy, not the 'not to use' wording.

Until the kubelet reconnected, the delete may not have reached the node, so the process can have outlived the API object. Confirm with kubectl describe node worker-b and kubectl get node -o yaml. On the broker template, set an explicit unreachable NoExecute toleration of tolerationSeconds 6000 (the local-state example) so a short partition does not evict it. Do not delete the PVC.
correct_alternative: Same eviction: the automatic unreachable toleration is 300 seconds, the describe shows Ready Unknown, and five minutes of that state removes ordinary pods. DaemonSets stay because their NoExecute toleration has no tolerationSeconds. Check the node with kubectl describe node and kubectl get node -o yaml; a Ready node may already have lost the taint. The process may have kept running on the partitioned node until the kubelet came back. Instead of 6000 seconds, put an explicit unreachable NoExecute toleration on the broker template and omit tolerationSeconds, so it stays bound for the whole partition the way a DaemonSet does. That also suppresses the automatic 300. Do not delete the PVC. Leaving the pod bound forever will not fail it over if the node never returns, so delete the pod yourself only if the node is actually gone.
generic: The node was NotReady, so cordon it and drain it. The broker likely OOMKilled or failed liveness; raise memory and check probes. If the new pod is slow, delete the PVC and let it provision again. DaemonSets are unrelated to broker restarts.
note: The describe layout follows the node debug page (Ready Unknown, NodeStatusUnknown, unreachable NoExecute and NoSchedule taints, tolerationSeconds 300). Host names, times, and which pods remained are invented. any_of m5a/m5b: 6000 is the documented local-state example; omitting tolerationSeconds keeps the pod bound forever, which also survives a short partition but does not fail the pod over if the node never returns. The concepts section still says the node lifecycle controller evicts when tolerationSeconds elapses; the taint-eviction section says that since 1.29 the actor is taint-eviction-controller. must.text: Main diagnosis: with whenUnsatisfiable DoNotSchedule, maxSkew is the maximum difference from the global minimum. A 2/2/1 zone layout has global minimum 1, so a zone that already has 2 pods cannot take another. The only zone under that cap has no Ready node, and DoNotSchedule leaves the pod Pending.
set_evidence: if you have 3 zones with 2, 2 and 1 matching pods respectively, `MaxSkew` is set to 1 then the global minimum is 1.
The field `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` tells the scheduler to let the incoming Pod stay pending if the scheduler can't find a way to satisfy the constraint.

must.text: Raises maxSkew (for example to 2) so a zone that already has two brokers can take the replacement while eu-central-1c is down.
set_evidence: Change `maxSkew` to a bigger value - such as `2` - so that the incoming Pod can be placed into zone `A` as well.

must.text: Or sets whenUnsatisfiable to ScheduleAnyway so the pod is still scheduled, with a preference for the topology domain that has fewer matching pods.
set_evidence: Change `whenUnsatisfiable: DoNotSchedule` to `whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway` to ensure the incoming Pod to be always schedulable (suppose other scheduling APIs are satisfied).

must.text: Does not blame the omitted minDomains. When minDomains is omitted the constraint behaves as if minDomains is 1, so the global minimum stays the smallest zone's pod count rather than being forced to 0.
set_evidence: If you do not specify `minDomains`, the constraint behaves as if `minDomains` is 1.

must.text: Checks that the candidate nodes actually have the topology.kubernetes.io/zone label. Nodes without the topology key's label are skipped, so an unlabeled node cannot hide this Pending pod.
set_evidence: the incoming Pod has no chances to be scheduled onto this kind of nodes

must_not.text: States that maxSkew 1 means each zone may hold at most one matching pod, so the zones that already have two brokers are already illegal.
must_not.condition: Counts when maxSkew is described as an absolute cap of one pod per zone. Describing it as the gap above the global minimum does not count.
must_not.near_miss: maxSkew 1 is the largest gap above the global minimum, which is 1 in this 2/2/1 layout, so a zone may already hold 2.

must_not.text: Removes topologySpreadConstraints so the Pending broker can be stacked into a zone that already has two brokers.
must_not.condition: Counts when the constraint is deleted as the remedy. ScheduleAnyway, or a larger maxSkew, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Keep the constraint and set whenUnsatisfiable to ScheduleAnyway, or raise maxSkew, so a later schedule still prefers an even zone spread.

reference: DoNotSchedule treats maxSkew as the largest gap above the global minimum. Three zones with 2, 2 and 1 pods have global minimum 1, so maxSkew 1 allows at most 2 in a zone. eu-central-1a and eu-central-1b are already at 2. eu-central-1c is the only legal zone and its node is NotReady, so the scheduler leaves payments-kafka-5 Pending. minDomains is omitted, which behaves as 1, and does not zero the global minimum. Confirm the nodes carry topology.kubernetes.io/zone; nodes without that label are skipped. Do not delete a Ready broker. Either raise maxSkew to 2, which allows a third pod in a and b while c is down, or set whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway, which still places the pod and prefers the thinner zone. Read-only: kubectl get pods -n payments -l app=payments-kafka -o wide and kubectl get nodes -L topology.kubernetes.io/zone.
correct_alternative: Leave maxSkew at 1 and set whenUnsatisfiable: ScheduleAnyway. The pod then schedules on a node in a or b that has CPU, with a preference for the domain that has fewer matching pods, instead of staying Pending until eu-central-1c returns. Do not delete the constraint and do not delete a Ready broker to manufacture skew. The omitted minDomains is behaving as 1 and is not the outage. Check the zone labels before changing the constraint.
generic: The Pending pod needs more CPU. Cordon the NotReady node, raise the broker requests, and add a node in eu-central-1c. maxSkew 1 means one pod per zone, so delete two brokers and let the scheduler start over. Topology spread does not block scheduling when a zone is down.
note: any_of m2a/m2b: either change schedules the pod while the small zone is down; m2a keeps a hard cap, m2b turns the cap into a preference. The FailedScheduling line is invented. Pod, zone, and label names are invented. The 2/2/1 numbers match the documented maxSkew example. Deleting a pod is a documented troubleshooting option for a stuck rollout and is not a must-not; it is a bad fit here because these are Kafka brokers, and neither branch requires it.

must.text: Main cause: RollingUpdate with the default OrderedReady policy stopped on orders-kafka-2, which never became Ready, and reverting the template does not repair it. The controller keeps waiting for that broken pod to become Ready, which never happens, before it will apply the good configuration.
set_evidence: StatefulSet will continue to wait for the broken Pod to become Ready (which never happens) before it will attempt to revert it back to the working configuration.

must.text: After the template is already back on orders-kafka:4.3.2, deletes the pods that were started with the bad configuration (orders-kafka-2 only). The StatefulSet then recreates them from the reverted template.
set_evidence: After reverting the template, you must also delete any Pods that StatefulSet had already attempted to run with the bad configuration.

must.text: Or sets updateStrategy to OnDelete, which does not auto-update pods, and deletes orders-kafka-2 so the controller creates a new pod from the current template.
set_evidence: Users must manually delete Pods to cause the controller to create new Pods that reflect modifications made to a StatefulSet's `.spec.template`.

must.text: Deletes only orders-kafka-2. RollingUpdate proceeds from the largest ordinal to the smallest, one pod at a time, and waits until the updated pod is Running and Ready before touching its predecessor, so orders-kafka-0 and orders-kafka-1 are still on 4.3.2.
set_evidence: It will proceed in the same order as Pod termination (from the largest ordinal to the smallest), updating each Pod one at a time.

must.text: Treats the omitted podManagementPolicy as OrderedReady, which is the default, rather than as Parallel.
set_evidence: `OrderedReady` pod management is the default for StatefulSets.

must.text: Verifies with kubectl rollout status statefulsets/orders-kafka --watch=false, which reports StatefulSet rollout status without waiting for the rollout to finish.
set_evidence: don't wait for rollout to finish, just check the status

must_not.text: Recommends scaling orders-kafka to 0, deleting the StatefulSet or its PersistentVolumeClaims, or setting updateStrategy Recreate, which deletes every broker pod and incurs downtime.
must_not.condition: Counts when scale-to-0, deleting the StatefulSet or its PVCs, or the Recreate strategy is the proposed fix. Deleting only orders-kafka-2, or switching to OnDelete and deleting that pod, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: OnDelete plus a manual delete of orders-kafka-2 recreates that one pod from the current template.

must_not.text: Says reverting the pod template is enough and the controller will move orders-kafka-2 back to 4.3.2 on its own.
must_not.condition: Counts if the revert alone is stated as sufficient. Saying the template must be the good image before the broken pod is deleted does not count.
must_not.near_miss: The template has to be orders-kafka:4.3.2 before orders-kafka-2 is deleted, or the recreate comes back on rc9.

reference: RollingUpdate walks ordinals from highest to lowest and waits until the updated pod is Running and Ready. orders-kafka-2 was first onto 4.3.2-rc9 and never became Ready, so 0 and 1 stayed on 4.3.2. podManagementPolicy is omitted, and OrderedReady is the default. With that policy, reverting the template is not enough: the controller waits for the broken pod to become Ready before it will apply the good template. The template is already orders-kafka:4.3.2, so delete only orders-kafka-2. The StatefulSet recreates it from the reverted template. Check with kubectl rollout status statefulsets/orders-kafka --watch=false and confirm the new pod is Ready on 4.3.2. Do not scale to 0, delete PVCs, or switch to Recreate, which deletes every pod.
correct_alternative: The stuck pod is the OrderedReady rollback bug: the controller will not put the reverted template onto orders-kafka-2 until that pod is Ready, and rc9 never is. Only the highest ordinal was updated. Set spec.updateStrategy.type to OnDelete so the controller stops trying to roll pods, then delete orders-kafka-2. OnDelete creates a replacement from the current template, which is already 4.3.2. Leave 0 and 1 alone. Confirm with kubectl rollout status statefulsets/orders-kafka --watch=false. Do not scale the set to 0 or delete claims.
generic: CrashLoopBackOff means the image or the memory limit is wrong. kubectl rollout undo the StatefulSet, raise memory, and wait. Once Git shows 4.3.2 the controller will roll the bad pod back by itself. Restart all three brokers if broker 2 stays down.
note: The pod table, images, and empty podManagementPolicy are invented. CrashLoopBackOff is a plausible status for a container that exits; the page's example is a bad binary or configuration that never becomes Ready. any_of m2a/m2b: delete the bad pod under RollingUpdate after the revert, or switch to OnDelete and delete that pod. Recreate is not in the group: it deletes every pod and the page says it incurs downtime. The forced-rollback section calls the wait a known issue. kubectl rollout undo is not the documented StatefulSet repair.

must.text: Main cause: the brokers mount the ConfigMap key as a subPath, and a container that uses a ConfigMap as a subPath volume mount does not receive ConfigMap updates. Waiting out another kubelet sync will not refresh that file.
set_evidence: A container using a ConfigMap as a subPath volume mount will not receive ConfigMap updates.

must.text: Rolls the payments-kafka pods so each new container mounts server.properties from the current ConfigMap, and keeps the subPath mount for later edits that will again require a roll.
must.source: inferred from container start mounting the current ConfigMap object
must.not_indexed_note: The ConfigMap page says a subPath mount does not receive updates. It does not say that recreating the pod rebuilds that mount from the current object; that follows from the mount being created when the container starts.

must.text: Or removes the subPath and mounts the ConfigMap as a directory (a pod template change, so the brokers roll), so later edits are projected into the pod after the kubelet sync.
set_evidence: When a ConfigMap currently consumed in a volume is updated, projected keys are eventually updated as well.
If you change the pod template for a workload resource, that resource needs to create replacement Pods that use the updated template.

must.text: Does not move num.network.threads to an environment variable and expect a live update. ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables are not updated automatically and still need a pod restart.
set_evidence: ConfigMaps consumed as environment variables are not updated automatically and require a pod restart.

must.text: Uses the debug pod as the check that the ConfigMap object is already new: a mount without subPath is refreshed on the kubelet periodic sync, with a delay up to the sync period plus cache propagation. That path is why the debug file shows 8 and the broker file does not.
set_evidence: The kubelet checks whether the mounted ConfigMap is fresh on every periodic sync.

must.text: Rolls back by restoring num.network.threads=3 in the ConfigMap and rolling the brokers again if 8 is the wrong value.
must.source: operational rollback of the ConfigMap key
must.not_indexed_note: Restoring a previous ConfigMap key is operational practice. The ConfigMap page does not describe reverting an edit.

must_not.text: Deletes ConfigMap broker-config so the pods remount it from scratch.
must_not.condition: Counts when the ConfigMap object is deleted as the way to refresh the file. Rolling pods, or dropping subPath, while leaving the ConfigMap in place does not count.
must_not.near_miss: Leave broker-config in place and roll the brokers, or drop the subPath, so they mount the current object.

must_not.text: States that every ConfigMap volume is immutable, so the debug pod showing 8 must be reading a different object.
must_not.condition: Counts when a normal ConfigMap volume is said never to update. Saying that only the subPath mount stays stale does not count.
must_not.near_miss: A ConfigMap volume without subPath is updated on the kubelet sync. The subPath mount is the one that stays at 3.

reference: The broker file stays at 3 because subPath mounts do not receive ConfigMap updates. The debug pod has no subPath, so the kubelet refreshes it on the periodic sync. The object has been new for 90 minutes; more waiting will not fix the brokers. Either roll payments-kafka so the subPath is created from the current ConfigMap (later edits still need a roll), or drop subPath and mount the directory so later edits project into the pod after the kubelet sync. Changing the pod template rolls the StatefulSet, which is the one restart this already-stale file needs. Do not switch the setting to an environment variable for a live update: env vars from a ConfigMap update only on restart. Do not delete broker-config. Verify by reading the file in the broker and comparing it to the ConfigMap. Roll back by putting 3 back in the ConfigMap and rolling again.
correct_alternative: Keep the subPath, which is what the process path expects, and roll the StatefulSet once so each new container mounts the current server.properties. Do not wait on the kubelet sync and do not delete the ConfigMap. Environment variables would also stay stale until a restart, so they are not a shortcut. Verify with grep inside the pod against kubectl get configmap broker-config. If 8 causes trouble, put 3 back and roll again. A later edit of this subPath will not appear until the next roll.
generic: ConfigMaps never update in a running pod. Restart the whole cluster, delete the ConfigMap, and recreate it. The debug pod is cached and should be ignored. Raise num.network.threads on the broker command line and reboot the nodes.
note: any_of m2a/m2b: a roll refreshes a subPath once; removing subPath is what makes later edits project without a dedicated refresh. m2a is not_indexed because the page does not spell out the recreate. m5 rollback is not_indexed. The exec output and the mount snippet are invented. The num.network.threads value is an invented broker setting, not a claim from the Kafka config pages.

must.text: States that a percentage maxUnavailable rounds the number of pods that may be disrupted up, so the count can exceed the written percentage. On 9 brokers, 30% rounds to 3 pods, not 2.
set_evidence: When you specify the value `maxUnavailable` as a percentage, Kubernetes rounds up the number of Pods that may be disrupted. Thereby a disruption can exceed your defined `maxUnavailable` percentage.

must.text: Sets maxUnavailable to the integer 2, a count of pods, so the cap is two brokers rather than a percentage that rounds up.
set_evidence: When you specify an integer, it represents a number of Pods.

must.text: Or sets minAvailable to the integer 7. On a fixed StatefulSet of 9 that is the same cap as maxUnavailable 2, the same way the documented size-3 budget can be written either way.
set_evidence: For example, if the above `zk-pdb` object selects the pods of a StatefulSet of size 3, both specifications have the exact same meaning.

must.text: Sets only one of maxUnavailable and minAvailable. A single PodDisruptionBudget cannot carry both.
set_evidence: You can specify only one of `maxUnavailable` and `minAvailable` in a single `PodDisruptionBudget`.

must.text: Warns that a percentage maxUnavailable still allows the last pod to be disrupted if the StatefulSet is scaled to one replica, which is an effective unavailability of 100%. An integer cap does not do that by percentage rounding.
set_evidence: If the total number of desired replicas is just one, that single replica is still allowed for disruption, leading to an effective unavailability of 100%.

must.text: Warns that the budget limits voluntary evictions only. A node failure can still take the set below the cap, so 30% or the integer 2 is not a hard promise that two brokers stay up.
set_evidence: The budget can only protect against voluntary evictions, not all causes of unavailability.

must_not.text: States that 30% of 9 allows at most 2 disruptions because Kubernetes truncates the percentage.
must_not.condition: Counts when the percentage is said to round down or to allow only 2 of these 9 pods. Saying the allowed count rounds up to 3 does not count.
must_not.near_miss: 30% of 9 rounds up, so the budget allows 3 voluntary disruptions, which is more than the author wanted.

must_not.text: Sets maxUnavailable to 0 so the parallel drain cannot take any broker down.
must_not.condition: Counts when maxUnavailable 0 or 0% is recommended as the safer cap. An integer maxUnavailable of 2, or minAvailable of 7, does not count.
must_not.near_miss: An integer maxUnavailable of 2 allows two voluntary disruptions and refuses a third. Zero means no voluntary eviction, and a drain of a node that runs one of these pods does not finish.

reference: maxUnavailable "30%" does not mean 2 of 9. Kubernetes rounds the number of pods that may be disrupted up, and a percentage can therefore exceed the written percent. 30% of 9 is 2.7, which rounds to 3, so three brokers may be voluntarily unavailable at once. For a hard cap of 2, set maxUnavailable: 2 (an integer) and leave minAvailable unset. Only one of those two fields is allowed. minAvailable: 7 is the same rule on this fixed size of 9, matching the documented equivalence of the two forms on a StatefulSet. Prefer to know that a percentage still moves with the replica count and, if the set is ever scaled to one pod, that one pod remains disruptable. The budget does not protect against a node crash. Selector app=payments-kafka stays as given, because it already matches the StatefulSet.
correct_alternative: Write minAvailable: 7 and omit maxUnavailable. On 9 pods that leaves two that may be disrupted, and for a fixed StatefulSet size the two integer forms mean the same thing. Do not also set maxUnavailable. Do not keep "30%": that rounds up to 3. Say explicitly that this integer minAvailable will not track a later replica change the way a percentage would, and that a node failure is outside the budget. If the set is scaled to one replica, do not switch back to a small percentage: that single replica is still allowed to be disrupted.
generic: Thirty percent of nine is about two pods, so the manifest is already the right cap. Add minAvailable: 90% next to it to be safer, and set maxUnavailable: 0 during the upgrade so no broker can be drained. PDBs also keep pods up when a node crashes.
note: any_of m2a/m2b: integer maxUnavailable 2 and integer minAvailable 7 are the same cap on a fixed size of 9. The step from 30% of 9 to 3 is arithmetic on the documented round-up (2.7 rounds to 3). The 7 is 9 minus 2. No point is flagged. The proposed manifest in the question is the object under review; nothing in it is a live cluster dump.

Explaining that the pair deletes and recreates, as a reason not to do it, does not count. Force=true,Replace=true on a Job that must rerun every sync does not count if the StatefulSet is explicitly excluded.

That is why the live image matches Git and nothing was deleted. Keep ServerSideApply=true: it is the one non-default option, and it is what sends kubectl apply --server-side --force-conflicts. Remove the Force=true annotation from the StatefulSet. Do not add Replace=true. Do not add Replace=true: it wins over ServerSideApply and the Force option then deletes and recreates the StatefulSet. The minimal non-default setting is ServerSideApply=true alone.

Run kubectl apply by hand, restart argocd-application-controller, and raise the sync timeout. ignoreDifferences on the image will stop the conflict from showing. Add more replicas if the brokers look unhealthy.

The question's sync outcome (server-side apply, no delete, live image matches Git) is what the sync-options page says Force=true does under ServerSideApply. No sync-log line is invented. must.text: Leaves kubelet probes alone. Once the brokers are isolated for ingress, connections from the pod's own node stay allowed, so no extra from entry is required for the node network.

must_not.near_miss: AND is one from element that holds both selectors. Two list items are OR.

The policy allows any pod in a namespace labeled kubernetes.io/metadata.name=billing, or any pod labeled app=ledger-producer in payments itself, to reach the brokers on TCP 9093. A bare podSelector means the NetworkPolicy's own namespace. Put both selectors in one from element so they AND: namespace kubernetes.io/metadata.name=billing and pod app=ledger-producer, port TCP 9093, policyTypes Ingress, podSelector app=payments-kafka. Do not split the selectors into two from items and do not add Egress.
generic: NetworkPolicy is a firewall around the namespace. Put the billing namespace and the producer label on separate from lines so both must match, and add Egress with no ports so the brokers are fully locked down. If probes fail, set the policy to allow 0.0.0.0/0. An empty podSelector on the policy is the same as selecting the brokers.

The OR and AND behavior is the documented from-list rule; the role=client / user=alice sentences are the page's own example of the same shape. No any_of. set_evidence: Resources are applied in ascending wave order, and Argo CD waits for each wave to become healthy before starting the next.

must.text: Puts the ConfigMap on the default wave or a negative wave, not a wave above the StatefulSet. Hooks and resources default to wave 0, and a negative wave runs before the others.
